subject: knit2html custom CSS only to a given chunk?

messages.author: d567d0ef3c054a35
messages.subject: knit2html custom CSS only to a given chunk?
parts:
Greetings. I've been experimenting with using the "pander" package to
generate HTML tables from R objects (a matrix in this case).

In brief, the drill is:

library(knitr)
library(markdown)
options(markdown.HTML.stylesheet="pander-table.css")
knit2html("pander-table.Rmd")

To begin with, I wanted to customize the table layout so as to give more
padding between table-data elements, but, of course, once you get to use your
own CSS, you can go crazy and put in background color, grid lines, etc.

This all works nicely for the table, but it has the unfortunate side effect of
removing the other, default formatting. The code chunks are missing the
shaded boxes in the HTML output, for instance.

Is there some way to apply the custom CSS ("pander-table.css") JUST to a given
chunk of code? I fiddled around with defining a CSS class, "pander", with the
appropriate table, tr, and td attributes, directly in the Rmd file and then
sandwiching the pander code chunk between:

<div class="pander">
.
.
.
</div>

That made things get REALLY ugly.

Any suggestions?

Thanks,

-- Mike

messages.author: 065110cca96a6373
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] knit2html custom CSS only to a given chunk?
parts:
Hi Mike,

I think that setting up your own class is the right approach.  If things 'get really ugly' I would say that is an issue with the HTML/CSS.  Part of the class definition may need to include clearing some elements you do not want, etc.

I write presentations in HTML5 + R + knitr and do things like this:

<section class="slide">
  <h2>2. MplusAutomation</h2>
<div class="mystyle"> <!-- this is a style I defined for tables -->
<!--begin.rcode echo=FALSE, results = "asis"
print(xtable(d3$table, caption = "Descriptive Statistics at Time 3"),
  type = "html", file = "", html.table.attributes=NULL,
  comment=FALSE, caption.placement="top")
end.rcode-->
</div>
</section>
If you also want the code echoed, you could put them in different chunks, so that you echo the code in a chunk not wrapped in your class, and only put the output in the div tag.

Cheers,

Josh

messages.author: cc1ef8c8158d6b73
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] knit2html custom CSS only to a given chunk?
parts:
It is easy to add extra CSS to the HTML output with the latest version
of the markdown package on CRAN -- use the 'header' argument instead
of 'stylesheet'; see ?markdown::markdownToHTML

In this case, all you need is

knit2html(..., header = c('<style type="text/css">',
readLines('pander-table.css'), '</style>'))

You can even customize the HTML template using the 'template'
argument; the default template is
https://github.com/rstudio/markdown/blob/master/inst/resources/markdown.html
You can use your own template so you can write anything in the HTML
header. This is basically how the knitBootstrap package works:
https://github.com/jimhester/knitrBootstrap/ e.g.
http://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/jimhester/knitrBootstrap/blob/master/inst/examples/all.html

Regards,
Yihui

Thanks, Yihui. I'm not sure why this approach works better than the other
one, but it does.

One still has to contend with possible interference between "markdown.css" and
the custom CSS file. For instance:

markdown.css
------------

body, td {
font-family: sans-serif;
background-color: white;
font-size: 12px;
margin: 8px;
}

I had:

pander-table.css
----------------

table {
border: 2px solid black;
background-color: LightGoldenRodYellow;
border-collapse: collapse;
}

td, th {
padding: 5px;
border: 1px solid LightBlue;
}

In that situation, only the table-header line in the output had the background
color of "LightGoldenRodYellow". I assume this was because in markdown.css the
td color was explicitly assigned as "white", while in pander-table.css it was
not explicitly specified. (I assumed it would be inherited from the
background for table.) Once I modified the stanza to:

td, th {
padding: 5px;
background-color: LightGoldenRodYellow;
border: 1px solid LightBlue;
}

the output was exactly what I wanted. I suppose this is all perfectly
obvious, but it may save somebody a headache.

-- Mike
